analysis.one_liner: Guarantees workers at mid-size and larger employers ten weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave for a new child or a child's serious illness.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a single cosponsor, never got a committee or Senate vote, and died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required employers covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act with 50 or more employees (dropping to 35 after three years) to give eligible workers up to ten workweeks of unpaid leave in any 24-month period after a birth, adoption, or foster placement, or to care for a child with a serious health condition [S3]. Workers could swap in accrued paid leave, and employers would have had to keep the worker's health insurance active during the leave and restore the worker to the same or an equivalent job afterward [S3]. A parallel title gave federal civil service employees the same rights [S2]. The Labor Department would enforce it through complaints, investigations, and civil suits, with damages for workers who were denied their rights [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Working parents and parents of seriously ill children at covered employers, who could take time off without losing their job or health coverage; single parents and mothers in particular, whom the bill's findings identify as bearing the brunt of caretaking without job protection [S3]. Federal employees would get the same entitlement [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Employees get an enforceable right to ten workweeks of leave in any 24-month period for the birth, adoption, foster placement, or serious health condition of a child, with the birth/adoption entitlement expiring six months after the event [S3].
Workers who take the leave keep their health insurance at the same level and must be restored to their old position or an equivalent one with the same pay and benefits [S3].
The bill is gender-neutral, letting fathers as well as mothers take leave, which its findings say reduces the incentive for employers to discriminate against women of childbearing age [S3].

Employers may not fire or discriminate against workers for using the leave or filing a complaint, and the Secretary of Labor can investigate and sue, with workers able to recover lost wages plus additional damages and attorney's fees [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers, who would hold jobs open, maintain health coverage for employees on leave, and handle notice, certification, and recordkeeping requirements; the costs would fall most directly on employers with 50 or more employees, and the threshold would drop to 35 employees after three years [S3].

drawbacks.text: The leave can be entirely unpaid, so a parent who cannot afford weeks without a paycheck may be unable to use the right; employees may only substitute accrued paid vacation or personal leave if they have it [S3].

Covered employers bear the cost of holding positions open and continuing group health coverage at full level during the leave, and the bill's coverage threshold tightens from 50 employees to 35 after three years, pulling more small employers into the mandate [S3].

The bill requires employers to cover the cost of second and third medical opinions when they doubt a leave request, to keep records, to post notices (with fines for willful violations), and to submit to Labor Department investigations and potential liquidated damages [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real but limited: job security, not income. A parent is guaranteed a job to come back to, but if they lack savings or accrued paid leave, ten unpaid weeks may be out of reach in practice. The main cost falls on employers in the form of staffing gaps and continued health coverage, which the bill tries to soften with notice rules, employer-paid second opinions, and a cap on how many weeks a married couple at the same company can combine. On balance, the protections are modest and targeted at a genuine gap—nothing in federal law at the time guaranteed a parent could take leave for a new child without risking the job.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 1989, sent to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, then passed to a subcommittee where it sat; no committee vote, no floor vote, and the two-year Congress ended with it dead.

narrative.text: Sen. Dennis DeConcini introduced the Parental Leave Act of 1989 on May 9, 1989 [S5].
The same day it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources [S5].

On May 17, 1989, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Children, Family, Drugs, and Alcohol, and the full committee requested executive comment from the Department of Labor, the Office of Personnel Management, and the Office of Management and Budget [S5].
No cosponsor ever joined the bill [S4].
There was no further action; the bill never left subcommittee and the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Covered employers avoided the cost of mandated leave and continued health coverage. Working parents got no federal leave guarantee from this bill, though Congress later enacted a similar and broader guarantee in 1993.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers avoided the mandate; parents waited

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and the bill had a single Democratic sponsor with no cosponsors from either party, so the record shows no measurable party split.

industries.industry: Employers with 50 or more employees (dropping to 35 after three years)
industries.note: These employers would have had to hold jobs open, keep health coverage active during leave, and comply with notice, certification, and enforcement rules [S3]. The benefit to workers—time off without losing the job—comes directly out of employer flexibility and cost.
Employers must maintain group health coverage at full level for employees on leave, so premiums continue flowing during absences [S3]. A minor effect.

They are excluded from the mandate in the bill's first three years, though the threshold would later drop to 35 employees [S3]. The bill directs the Labor Department to study effects on businesses with fewer than 50 employees [S2].
